strengths: The approach addresses a relevant restoration problem with a plausible combination of compact WavTokenizer representations and absorbing-state discrete diffusion.
Results on MusicNet show promising performance for longer gaps: the reported FAD at 300 ms is 3.81 versus approximately 4.9 for CQT-Diff+.
Preserving the observed waveform and applying a 10 ms boundary crossfade are sensible implementation choices. Evaluation includes three complementary objective metrics and several gap durations.
weaknesses: The contribution primarily combines existing tokenization, transformer, and score-entropy diffusion methods. No new objective or substantial algorithmic innovation is established, and no ablations demonstrate why discrete diffusion is preferable to simpler token-completion methods.

The abstract claims an MTG evaluation extending to 500 ms, and the conclusion claims strong performance at that duration, but the manuscript provides neither an MTG experimental setup nor corresponding results. Presented evidence covers only MusicNet gaps up to 300 ms.

Comparative validity is insufficiently established. The text references previously reported CQT-Diff+ results without clarifying whether baselines were rerun on identical excerpts with identical preprocessing and metric implementations. Relevant learned baselines discussed in the paper, including MAID and GACELA, are absent.

Evaluation uses only 60 short classical-music excerpts with fixed gap locations, without uncertainty estimates, repeated sampling, or listening tests. ODG values around -3.0 to -3.3 indicate substantial perceptual degradation under the paper's own scale, weakening claims of high perceptual quality. The promised audio-example link is missing.

Critical implementation details are omitted: transformer dimensions and parameter count, tokenizer checkpoint, noise schedule, reverse sampler and step count, and precise context-conditioning procedure. Waveform-to-token mask alignment is also unspecified. Because training masks clean-audio tokens whereas inference encodes corrupted waveforms, the effect of encoder receptive fields on neighboring context tokens requires explanation and validation.

Metric reporting needs clarification, including whether LSD and ODG cover entire excerpts or only repaired regions, the FAD reference population, and the log convention and numerical stabilization for LSD. Figure 3 also contradicts the blanket claim of superiority across all metrics: at 50 ms, AIDD has substantially worse ODG than CQT-Diff+.

There are no codec-reconstruction controls or ablations of tokenization, diffusion, and crossfading, so the source of improvements remains unclear. Claims of greater training stability, semantic coherence, and reduced artifacts are not directly evaluated.

strengths: Addresses a useful audio restoration problem with a plausible pipeline combining compact WavTokenizer representations, discrete diffusion, and waveform reconstruction.
Reports promising longer-gap results on MusicNet, including a 300 ms FAD of 3.81 versus approximately 4.9 reported for CQT-Diff+.
Preserving observed waveform samples and applying boundary crossfades are sensible practical choices. Evaluation includes three complementary objective metrics.
weaknesses: The contribution largely combines existing WavTokenizer, DiT, and score-entropy diffusion components. No substantive new modeling mechanism or analysis establishes an advance beyond applying these components to inpainting.

The abstract claims MTG evaluation up to 500 ms, and the conclusion claims strong 500 ms performance, but the manuscript provides neither the corresponding experimental setup nor results. The documented evaluation covers only MusicNet gaps up to 300 ms.

Comparison validity is insufficiently established: Section 6 references previously reported CQT-Diff+ results without clarifying whether baselines were rerun on identical clips, corruptions, preprocessing, and metric implementations. MAID and relevant long-gap generative baselines discussed in related work are absent.

Evaluation uses only 60 short test clips with fixed gap locations, without confidence intervals, repeated runs, or listening tests. FAD on this small sample and objective perceptual proxies provide limited support for claims of robust perceptual quality and semantic coherence.

There are no ablations separating the effects of discrete diffusion, the pretrained codec, and crossfading. Comparisons with simpler token completion models and a codec reconstruction reference are needed to establish why the proposed formulation helps.

Important implementation details are missing, including transformer dimensions, parameter count, tokenizer checkpoint, diffusion schedule, sampling algorithm and step count, and precise masking and conditioning procedures. Waveform-to-token gap alignment and the codec's temporal receptive field are particularly important because training masks clean tokens while inference encodes corrupted audio.

The blanket claim of outperforming CQT-Diff+ across all metrics is overstated: Figure 3 shows substantially worse short-gap ODG. Some plotted AIDD values also appear inconsistent with Table 1, notably the 300 ms FAD. These discrepancies require reconciliation.

Claims of greater training stability, reduced artifacts, and efficient modeling lack direct measurements. No inference latency or memory comparison is provided, and the promised audio-example link is missing.

strengths: The paper addresses a useful restoration problem with a plausible combination of compact audio tokens and discrete diffusion. Modeling approximately 75 tokens per second offers an attractive alternative to waveform-level generation.

The reported MusicNet results suggest promise for longer gaps: Table 1 reports FAD 3.81 at 300 ms, compared with approximately 4.9 cited for CQT-Diff+, and Figure 3 suggests improved ODG at larger gaps.

Preserving the original waveform outside the reconstructed region and applying boundary crossfades are sensible engineering choices. Evaluation includes complementary spectral and perceptual proxy metrics.
weaknesses: Central experimental claims lack supporting results. The abstract claims evaluation on MTG with gaps up to 500 ms, and the conclusion emphasizes strong 500 ms performance, but the manuscript provides neither an MTG protocol nor corresponding results. The documented evaluation covers only 60 MusicNet excerpts and gaps up to 300 ms.

The comparison does not establish superiority reliably. Section 6 cites previously reported baseline values without clarifying whether baselines were rerun on identical excerpts, gaps, preprocessing, and metric implementations. Relevant methods discussed in the paper, including MAID and GACELA, are absent from the experiments.

The contribution primarily combines existing WavTokenizer, DiT, and score-entropy diffusion components. No ablations or controlled comparisons establish the benefit of discrete diffusion over simpler token completion, or separate its contribution from the pretrained codec and crossfading. Claims of improved stability, semantic coherence, and reduced spectral artifacts are consequently insufficiently supported.

Essential implementation details are missing: transformer dimensions and parameter count, tokenizer checkpoint and audio preprocessing, noise schedule, reverse sampler and sampling steps, and the precise conditioning procedure. The mapping from waveform gaps to token masks is particularly important because encoding corrupted audio can also affect surrounding tokens; this training–inference mismatch is not analyzed.

The numerical reporting needs reconciliation. Figure 3 appears inconsistent with Table 1, notably for FAD at 100 and 300 ms. The statement that AIDD outperforms CQT-Diff+ across all metrics is also too broad: the plotted ODG is worse at 50 ms, and FAD is not consistently better at shorter gaps.

Perceptual-quality claims rely exclusively on objective proxies, with no listening study and no usable audio-example link. Reported ODG values around -3.0 to -3.3 indicate substantial distortion on the paper's own scale. FAD is estimated from a small evaluation set without uncertainty estimates, and it is unclear whether metrics cover gaps alone or entire excerpts containing preserved audio.
Overall, the promising application idea is not supported by sufficiently complete, reproducible, and controlled evidence to meet a top-tier conference acceptance threshold.

strengths: The paper addresses a useful audio restoration problem with a sensible combination of pretrained audio tokenization and discrete diffusion. Compact token sequences provide a plausible basis for modeling musical context efficiently.

MusicNet results are promising: at 300 ms, AIDD reduces FAD from 4.652 to 3.549 and LSD from 0.324 to 0.297 relative to CQT-Diff+, while improving ODG. Evaluation spans two datasets and several gap lengths.
The ablations examine both proposed training components separately and together, including several regularization weights and first- versus second-order differences.
weaknesses: The span-based forward process is not reconciled with the diffusion mathematics. Equations 2–4 use tokenwise absorbing transitions, whereas Section 4.3 introduces correlated span corruption with a fixed masking budget. Matching the overall masked proportion does not establish the required conditional probability ratios or reverse transition rates. A compatible joint process and objective, or a clear explanation of the approximation, is needed.

The derivative loss is insufficiently specified. The paper does not explain how predicted embeddings are obtained differentiably from concrete scores, which embedding space is used, or whether its parameters are frozen. Moreover, matching ground-truth embedding derivatives is not equivalent to enforcing smoothness, and the assumed relationship between token-space geometry and perceptual continuity is not established.

The evidence for perceptual quality and long-range semantic coherence is limited. There is no listening study or direct musical-coherence evaluation, and the longest evaluated gap is 750 ms. At that length, the ODG advantage over bin2bin-MIDI is only 0.017, with reported dispersions around 0.5–0.6 and no paired significance analysis. MusicNet FAD is estimated from only 60 source segments without uncertainty estimates.

Comparisons do not isolate the contribution of discrete diffusion from the pretrained tokenizer. Missing controls include a straightforward masked-token completion model using the same tokenizer and a continuous latent diffusion alternative. MAID, discussed as a relevant diffusion method for long music gaps, is not evaluated. It is also unclear whether MAESTRO baselines were evaluated on the exact same randomly selected test subset.

The claim that the combined method consistently performs best is contradicted by Table 3. At 300 ms, derivative-only training achieves better FAD, span-only training achieves better LSD, and a derivative-only variant achieves better ODG than the reported combined configuration. The base model also receives 400k training steps versus 100k for other variants, preventing a controlled attribution of differences to the training components.

Reproducibility remains inadequate in the supplied manuscript. The appendix omits MAESTRO subset sizes and identities, architecture dimensions, tokenizer checkpoint, a clear audio sampling rate, noise schedule, and a sufficiently explicit inference sampler. The mapping from waveform gaps to token masks is particularly important given encoder receptive fields. Code is stated to accompany the submission, but it is not available in the supplied materials.

The novelty and efficiency claims exceed the supporting evidence. The principal architecture combines established WavTokenizer, DiT, and score-entropy diffusion components, while differentiation from prior discrete audio diffusion and masked-token modeling is limited. Claims of reduced model size, training cost, and data requirements lack a controlled accounting of tokenizer pretraining, total system parameters, and inference cost.

strengths: The token-space formulation is a promising approach to music inpainting, combining compact pretrained audio representations with discrete diffusion and practical waveform boundary handling.
Table 1 reports meaningful improvements over CQT-Diff+ on MusicNet: at 300 ms, FAD improves from 4.652 to 3.549, with improvements in LSD and ODG. The 375 ms MAESTRO result is also encouraging.
The experiments cover two datasets, several gap lengths, and complementary objective metrics. Ablations investigate both proposed training modifications and multiple hyperparameter settings.
weaknesses: The span-corruption formulation has an unresolved theoretical gap. Section 3 derives the objective and sampler using independent token transitions, whereas Section 4.3 introduces correlated masking with a prescribed budget. Matching the expected masked-token count does not establish the same joint corruption distribution or transition ratios. The paper does not derive a compatible sequence-level process, objective, or reverse sampler.

The derivative loss is insufficiently specified. The paper does not explain how predicted embeddings are obtained differentiably from concrete-score outputs, which embedding space is used, or whether those embeddings are fixed. Moreover, matching ground-truth embedding differences does not itself establish perceptual smoothness; that connection needs evidence.

The evaluation does not convincingly establish superiority for long gaps or semantic coherence. At 750 ms, the ODG improvement over bin2bin-MIDI is only 0.017, against reported variability of approximately 0.5–0.6, without sample counts or significance analysis. There is no listening study or direct musical-coherence evaluation, and gaps never exceed 750 ms.

Baseline coverage does not isolate the main contribution. MAID is discussed but not evaluated, and there is no matched token-based completion baseline using the same pretrained codec. Consequently, the experiments cannot distinguish benefits of discrete diffusion from benefits of the representation and pretraining.

The ablations do not support the claim that combining the modifications consistently performs best. At 300 ms, derivative-only training achieves better FAD than every combined variant; span-only training achieves better LSD. The base model also receives 400k training steps versus 100k for the variants, weakening controlled attribution. Independent training-seed uncertainty is not reported.

Reproducibility and comparison fairness remain unclear. The supplement omits MAESTRO subset sizes and identities, model dimensions, tokenizer checkpoint, noise schedule, and clear inference settings. It does not establish whether all baselines were evaluated on the same randomly selected MAESTRO test subset. Code is mentioned as a separate submission attachment but was not available in the supplied material.

Several claims exceed the evidence. Efficiency comparisons omit codec overhead and measured inference costs; stability and long-range coherence are not directly tested. The novelty is primarily an application and adaptation of existing components, and the broad first-use claims need more careful positioning against prior discrete audio diffusion.

strengths: The approach is well motivated: combining a compact pretrained audio tokenizer with discrete diffusion offers a practical formulation of music inpainting as conditional token completion.
MusicNet results are promising. At 300 ms, AIDD improves FAD from 4.652 to 3.549 and LSD from 0.324 to 0.297 relative to CQT-Diff+, while improving ODG across all evaluated MusicNet gap lengths.
Evaluation covers two datasets and several established baselines. The MAESTRO result at 375 ms shows a substantial numerical ODG improvement over the strongest reported baseline.

The ablations examine span masking, derivative regularization, their combination, and multiple hyperparameter settings, providing useful evidence that the proposed modifications can improve the base model.
weaknesses: The span-corruption formulation has an unresolved theoretical gap. Section 3 derives the objective and sampler for independent token transitions, whereas Section 4.3 introduces correlated span masking without deriving the corresponding joint transition process or showing that the same score targets and reverse sampler remain valid. Matching the expected masking fraction does not establish this equivalence; the masking budget also uses sigma(t) where the earlier formulation uses cumulative noise.

The derivative loss is insufficiently specified. The paper does not explain how predicted embeddings are obtained differentiably from concrete scores, which embedding space is used, or precisely which neighboring positions enter the loss. It also does not establish that distances and temporal derivatives in that embedding space reliably correspond to perceptual audio continuity.

Baseline comparability is unclear. The MAESTRO training and test subsets have neither sizes nor identities reported, and it is unclear whether all baselines were evaluated on the same selected recordings. MAID, a directly relevant conditional diffusion baseline discussed in the paper, is absent. A matched tokenizer-based completion baseline would help isolate the contribution of discrete diffusion from the pretrained representation.

Claims about perceptual quality and long-range semantic coherence exceed the evidence. There is no listening study or direct musical-consistency evaluation, and gaps extend only to 750 ms. At 750 ms, the ODG advantage over bin2bin-MIDI is just 0.017, with substantial reported variability and no paired significance analysis. MusicNet FAD is also worse than CQT-Diff+ at 150 ms.

The ablations do not support the claim that the combined method consistently performs best: standalone span masking obtains better LSD at both tested lengths, and derivative-only training obtains better FAD at 300 ms. The base model also receives 400k training steps versus 100k for the variants, and seed variability and the validation-based model-selection procedure are not reported.

Reproducibility and efficiency evidence are incomplete. The manuscript omits key architecture dimensions, a clearly specified inference schedule and sampler, the waveform-to-token masking rule, and sufficient metric aggregation details. Claims of half the model size and one-quarter the training time lack a controlled comparison accounting for tokenizer pretraining and inference cost. Supplementary code is mentioned but was not available in the supplied material.

The contribution is primarily an application of established tokenizer, transformer, and discrete score-entropy components with two relatively modest training modifications. The promising numerical results do not yet overcome the methodological and evaluation gaps sufficiently for acceptance at a top-tier AI conference.
